extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, geometers, and students/historians of classical geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Classical/ancient-geometry constructions and analyses for inscribing a triangle or polygon in a given circle so that the sides (or their extensions) pass through specified given points; includes lemmas, case classifications, and construction techniques (parallels, tangents, fixed-segment properties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Castillon's Problem (three given points A,B,C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem. Three points, A, B, C, being given, to inscribe a triangle DEF in the given circle, so that its sides shall pass through the given points A, B, C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis: Suppose done; let E,F be intersections of AD,BD with circle; draw FG ∥ AB, join EG meeting AB in K. From relationships (parallel angles, cyclic quadrilaterals) derive BA·AK = DA·AE so K is determined. Through centre L draw KL to get ratio NK:KM (given). Use Pappus' ratio NQ:QM :: NK:KM to locate Q, hence one leg EO passes through given Q and the other through C. Construct by reversing the analysis; demonstration is a reversal of the analysis (sometimes resorting to reductio ad absurdum if necessary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumeration of positional cases for three points relative to circle
rubrics_metrics.description: The different relative positions of the points A, B, C with respect to the circle and to each other give rise to several varieties of case, which will require some modifications of the analysis and composition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text lists multiple distinct cases (e.g., one point inside and another outside giving two solutions; coincidences of K and S; AB passing through center; special cases yielding tangents or known propositions such as Euclid III.36). A complete construction must enumerate and adapt to these cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good 'determination' criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: “Mais la determination n'est bonne que lorsqu'elle épargne une partie considerable de la construction; et j'avoue que je n'en ai pas pu trouver de telle pour ce probleme.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A determination (i.e., an additional datum fixing an otherwise indeterminate choice) is considered useful only if it spares a considerable part of the construction. Determinations that do not reduce construction effort are of limited value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of parallels and fixed-segment ratios (Castillon/Fuss style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct auxiliary parallels (e.g. FG ∥ AB, BG ∥ DE, BI ∥ HF) and use cyclic/parallel similarities to derive equalities of products of segments (EC·EA = ED·EH, HC·HF = HK·HG, etc.), which show certain points (H, K, etc.) are determined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method proceeds by repeated use of similarity and products of segments to reduce the problem to determining a chord/tangent known in magnitude and position; then reconstruct the triangle by reversing analysis. This style is typical of Fuss and Castillon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler's fixed-point/tangent properties (used in constructions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Several properties: (1) For line ADP meeting circle at P, D, the circle PDB described cuts AB always in the same point K (independent of P). (2) If OL ⟂ AB and LC equals tangent from L to circle, then any tangent from any point on AB equals AC. (3) KH is bisected in L. (4) Rectangle KA·HB equals square of KC or CH. (5) Triangles ACK and HCB are equiangular. (6) Algebraic forms AK = (AO^2 - r^2)/AB used to express AK.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties give invariant points/relationships (fixed K, equal tangents, midpoints, product equalities) that can be exploited to build constructions and reduce unknowns to given quantities; Euler often expresses results algebraically though geometric interpretations are supplied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler's construction approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Let O be centre, A,B,C given; set radius =1 and use algebraic relations (take BF = (something), define FK, FQ, etc.), then draw radius OW bisecting angle BFC by FS, draw mb ∥ FS meeting circle; that point is one vertex of required triangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euler's construction blends algebraic parameter choices with geometric steps (cosine/bisected angles, parallels) and relies on previously proved invariant properties; no full synthetic proof is always given but the construction follows from the earlier theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fuss's method (analysis then construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis: Use parallels and cyclic relations to get EC·EA = ED·EH and HF·HK = HC·HG, then show H and K are given since ED, EO, OM are given etc. Construction: join DE, make EH = given expression, set HK = given expression, take HB = MO, draw perpendicular RS and describe circle of radius HS; draw tangent KT from K to it meeting the given circle in I,G and proceed to construct B, A, C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fuss's 'demonstration' is largely analysis; construction follows by reversing analysis with explicit metric choices. He provides corollaries for cases when given points are inside/outside circle and notes multiple possible cases depending on which tangent is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lexell/Ottajano variations and incompleteness warning
rubrics_metrics.description: Lexell attempted Lagrange's formulae and gave complex constructions mixing trigonometrical and geometric reasoning. Ottajano produced constructions and several new problem variants but often failed to enumerate cases fully (considered 'incomplete').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting a solution, pay attention to complete case enumeration and to distinguish analysis from synthesis: Ottajano's work is valued for sagacity but criticized for incomplete case handling; a full solution should state all case distinctions and 'determinations'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ottajano's problem family (I–V)
rubrics_metrics.description: I. In a given circle to inscribe a triangle whose sides shall pass through three given collinear points. II. In a given circle to inscribe a triangle whose sides shall pass through three given points arbitrarily placed. III–V. Varied problems where two sides pass through given points and the third side makes a given angle with a line to a third point; one side passes through a given point and other two sides make given angles with lines to two other given points; given angle conditions between lines from vertices to given points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are distinct problem variants; methods and constructions differ and require careful statement of givens and enumeration of cases (points inside/outside, coincident positions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Malfatti's general polygon construction (lemma-based)
rubrics_metrics.description: General problem: In a given circle to inscribe a rectilineal figure of any given number of sides whose sides, being produced, may pass through as many given points however situated. Construction proceeds by joining successive given points and drawing parallels to generate a polygon MRSTU... whose angles correspond, then using parity rules (odd/even number of sides) to determine the key vertex M.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Malfatti provides two lemmas necessary for odd- and even-sided polygons (Lemma I: through two given points draw lines meeting circumference so that the line joining other intersections is parallel to given line; Lemma II: through two given points to inflect lines to a point on circumference so they contain a given angle). Follow stepwise: join AB, draw MR ∥ AB, etc., iterate parallels; deduce arc sums to locate M. The method reduces the general polygon to repeated triangle/quadrilateral steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parity (odd vs even number of sides) rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The slight difference in the final part for odd and even numbers of sides: when the polygon is odd-sided the line determining the principal point of the construction touches a determinable circle; when even-sided, the corresponding line is parallel to a determinable line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This parity distinction is of perpetual occurrence in polygon inquiries and affects whether an arc (and hence a vertex) is directly determined or determined only after considering a supplementary parallel/extension; constructions must adapt accordingly (Malfatti's explanation and Castillon/Fuss methods account for this).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction-to-lemma strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce complex inscription problems to simpler lemmas (e.g., inscribing a triangle with third side parallel to given line; constructing lines through two given points meeting circumference so that chord joining other intersections is parallel to a given line).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The general strategy across authors is to reduce general n-sided problems to repeated applications of two-point/triangle lemmas, then reassemble via parallels/tangents. Presenting these lemmas explicitly and proving them is central to a usable construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical-practice criterion: analysis considered as solution
rubrics_metrics.description: Many continental writers (and some modern commentators) content themselves with giving merely the analysis of the problem — evidently considering that in ancient geometry a problem was solved when the analysis had been effected; they often omitted the synthetic construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating historical solutions, note whether the author provided synthesis (construction) or only analysis; for practical constructibility, synthesis (explicit steps) and case enumeration are necessary even if analysis demonstrates existence/form of solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case-specific solvability statements (example)
rubrics_metrics.description: When one of the points C, Q is within the circle and the other without, the configuration is always possible, and two different triangles will fulfil the conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explicit solvability claims for positional configurations in a solution: state when solutions are unique, when there are two, and when constructions must be modified; these are part of a complete answer.
